name: feature-toggle
intent: Ship both the old and the new behaviour in one artifact and let a named runtime switch, read from configuration, pick the live path - so releasing a change is decoupled from deploying code, and a feature can be thrown on or off without a rebuild, a redeploy or a restart.
problem: A behaviour must be reachable by some users, environments or tenants and withheld from others, and it must be possible to change that decision faster than a build-and-deploy cycle allows - while half-finished work must not block a release and an incident must have a faster escape hatch than a rollback. Doing this by branching, by separate builds per customer, or by hard-wired configuration in the code multiplies the code that must be maintained and tested; doing it with an ad-hoc boolean inside the code couples the decision to the code that makes it.
context: Continuous delivery and trunk-based development, where deployment happens often and features are exposed on a different schedule; long-running services that must be operated (degraded, switched off, ramped up) without a restart; experiments, canaries and tiered or tenant-specific offerings where the audience of a code path is data, not code. The pattern applies to one code path plus its configuration source, and is decided together with the flag's lifetime and dynamism - release, ops, experiment or permission flag - because that choice dictates whether the state may live in a versioned file or needs a runtime store.
benefits: Deployment and release are decoupled: one build reaches every environment and the live behaviour is chosen by configuration, so shipping the code no longer exposes the feature.
Trunk-based development becomes practical - incomplete work is merged behind an off-by-default flag instead of living in a long-lived branch that diverges further every day.
Operations gain a kill switch: an ops flag restores the previous path in seconds without a rollback deploy and enables graceful degradation while a fix is prepared.
Progressive delivery: a canary or percentage rollout, then a cohort, then everyone, and an experiment flag that measures the effect of both variants on real traffic.
Packaging and entitlement: a permission flag turns a capability into a tier, a beta programme or a per-tenant option without a separate build per customer.
Both paths stay testable in one artifact: tests force the flag on and off instead of building and maintaining two variants.
tradeoffs: Toggle debt: a flag that outlives its rollout leaves permanently dead code and a configuration key nobody dares change; removing the flag afterwards is the expensive half of the life cycle.
Combinatorial testing: n independent flags create 2^n live configurations, so the matrix is sampled rather than covered and flag interactions are discovered in production.

Configuration drift: the same binary behaves differently per environment because a key is missing, misspelled or overridden locally, and the state of a running system cannot be reconstructed from the code alone.
Staleness and inconsistency: flags cached per process or per request mean a flip reaches instances at different times, and work already in flight can straddle the change.

Control-plane coupling: evaluating flags against a remote service puts that service in the request path, adding latency and a new availability dependency (in-process caches and defaults are the mitigation, and the reason to prefer the simplest binding time that works).

Security surface: a flag guarding unreleased or privileged behaviour is an access-control point, and per-request override mechanisms (query parameter, cookie, header) become attacker-influenced if they survive into production.
Indirection at the toggle point: unless the decision is encapsulated, conditionals accrete at call sites, each adding a configuration read and a branch to a hot path.

participants.responsibility: The code site that asks the router and dispatches to one of the two (or more) paths; keep it as few and as narrow as possible, and replace a repeated conditional with polymorphic substitution so the flag is interrogated once.
Resolves a named flag to a decision - on/off or a variant - from the toggle configuration and the toggle context; the only component that knows where and how flag state is stored.
The externalised state of every flag (versioned configuration file, database, or distributed key-value store) together with the defaults and overrides that govern an environment.
The per-decision inputs that non-boolean routing needs: user or tenant identity, cohort or group, percentage bucket, time window, request attributes.
The console, CLI or API through which operators and product owners change flag state, with the permissions and audit trail that make a flip reviewable and reversible.

use_cases: Release a multi-sprint feature: the work is merged behind an off-by-default release flag and exposed independently of the next deploy. Netflix uses this to decouple backend API releases from frontend deployments.

Canary and percentage rollout of a risky change, then full rollout, then deletion of the flag in the same sprint as the cleanup task. Facebook uses this approach to enable weekly or daily release trains with gradually increasing exposure.

Ops kill switch and load shedding: an ops flag disables a fragile or expensive path (an evolution of the circuit breaker) without a redeploy. Shopify uses ops flags to handle flash sales and Black Friday traffic spikes.

A/B experiments in which each user must be assigned to one cohort consistently for the whole test, so the toggle context, not chance, decides. Optimizely and Google Optimize standardize this via consistent hashing on user IDs.

Packaging, entitlement and per-tenant capability in a multi-tenant product where the same code serves customers with different contracts. SaaS platforms like Salesforce and HubSpot use permission flags for tiered feature access.

Stepwise migration (dual-write, dual-read, cutover, rollback) where the flag is both the cutover switch and the rollback switch. Amazon uses this pattern extensively for database migration with zero-downtime cutover.

Dark launch: deploy the new code path behind a release flag at 0% exposure, run it under real production load silently, observe error rates and latency, then progressively ramp — all without any user seeing the new behaviour. Google uses dark launch to validate Search ranking changes before any user impact.

Stepwise database migration (expand-contract pattern): add a new column behind a flag, backfill data with both columns live, flip the read path to the new column, verify, then remove the old column — the flag is both the cutover switch and the rollback switch. Uber uses this pattern with Piranha-generated cleanup diffs for schema migrations.

Seasonal or event-driven capability: a capacity or feature flag toggled on for a product launch, campaign, or peak trading period (e.g. Black Friday) and toggled off again afterward, with the same binary serving year-round. Etsy uses this for event-driven feature ramps.

Kill-switch driven graceful degradation: when a downstream dependency fails (database, payment processor, recommendation engine), an ops flag lets operations disable the fragile path instantly without a restart, serving a degraded but functional response to all users. Netflix applies this pattern for circuit-breaking individual microservices.

Shadow mode validation: run the new implementation in parallel with the old in production, comparing outputs (logging or metrics) but returning the old result to users — validates correctness before any user-visible exposure. Spotify uses shadow mode to validate payments system migrations.

Progressive technical migration: replace a module incrementally by routing portions of traffic through the new implementation behind a flag, expanding scope based on observed error rates, until the old implementation can be retired. Twitter/X used this to migrate timeline ranking algorithms without service disruption.

Deterministic bucketed ramp: hash the flag key, a salt and the user identifier into a stable bucket, then widen the bucket range from 0% to 100% so the same users stay in the target group at every step of the rollout. LaunchDarkly documents this with hash partitions of 1-100,000 derived from context key, flag key and salt.

Vendor-neutral toggle point: standardise the flag-evaluation API behind one interface so application code can switch between a commercial vendor, an open-source flag server or an in-house router without touching call sites. OpenFeature, a CNCF incubating project, specifies this API and ships SDKs across languages.
avoid_when: The change ships in a single release anyway: a plain deploy, or a keystone interface that hides the entry point until the last commit, is simpler than a flag plus its whole life cycle.
The difference is per-installation and permanent: an ordinary configuration value or a build variant is the honest model, not a toggle that will never be removed.

The decision is genuinely build-time (optional integration, platform variant, paid feature compiled out): use the compiler or build system (C preprocessor, Cargo features, build flavours) instead of a runtime router nobody switches at runtime.
No one owns flag hygiene: without an owner, an expiry and a removal task, each flag becomes permanent configuration debt, and a release train or short-lived branch is the lesser evil.
The guarded behaviour is a security decision: enforce it in the access-control layer, because a flag whose state is externally mutable is a weaker control than an authorization check.
anti_patterns: Long-lived release toggles that are never removed, leaving permanently dead branches that no test exercises and no one owns.
Nested flag conditions ("if A and not B or C") that make the live behaviour unreconstructable from the source; replace them with one decision object or polymorphic substitution.
Per-request flag overrides exposed in production (query parameter, cookie, header), so anyone can switch a feature on.
Flags named after implementation details ("useNewCheckoutImplV2") rather than capabilities, so nobody can judge whether they may be removed.
A flag service in the synchronous request path with no cache, no timeout and no fallback: an incident in the control plane becomes an outage of the product.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: the decision point asks, the router decides, the configuration owns state - and domain code knows none of the three.
Open/closed principle: a new feature arrives as new code behind a new flag instead of an edit to the release process.
Dependency inversion: inject the decision (a boolean, a function or a decision object) so business code does not depend on the toggling mechanism.
Single source of truth and configuration as code: flag state is versioned, reviewed and shipped like code, with explicit defaults.
Least surprise at the toggle point: one narrow, named decision per feature rather than scattered conditionals.
best_practices: Give every flag an owner, an expiry or review date and a removal task; delete the flag and its dead branch as soon as the rollout completes.
Keep toggle points few and narrow - wrap the decision in one named method, strategy or decision object so the conditional appears once.
Make the off state the safe default, so a missing key, a stale cache or a failed provider fails closed.
Keep flags out of the domain model: pass the decision into business code rather than letting it reach for a flag registry.
Test both paths and the combinations of flags that are live together, and treat a flag key as part of the interface you must not break silently.
Restrict per-request overrides to development and test; production flips go through the administrative path with an audit trail.
Prefer the earliest binding time that satisfies the requirement (build, start-up, runtime) because every step later widens the configuration space and the failure modes.

Use a dedicated feature-flag SDK or library rather than ad-hoc boolean flags in code — a purpose-built toggle router handles binding time, caching, default fallback, and audit trail in one place, and tests can mock it without dragging in the whole infrastructure.

Separate read and write APIs for flag management: operators write flag state through a governed API with authentication and audit logging, while evaluation engines read flag state through a separate, low-latency read path — preventing flag flips from competing with request-latency-sensitive evaluation in the same control plane.

Automate flag hygiene with dedicated tooling: run periodic cleanup sprints, use tools like Uber's Piranha (AST-based, generates deletion diffs for stale flags in Objective-C, Java, Swift) or LLM-driven workflows like DoorDash's multi-agent system that automates the full stale-flag cleanup loop from Jira issue to merge-ready PR.
sources: Pete Hodgson, Martin Fowler, "Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags)", https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html (2017) — Definitive taxonomy of toggle types (release, ops, experiment, permission), toggle router, toggle configuration and toggle context; covers toggle debt, testing strategies, and the keystone interface alternative.

Martin Fowler, "FeatureFlag (bliki)", https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/FeatureFlag.html (2010) — Build-time versus run-time toggles, release flags, and the keystone interface pattern for hiding incomplete features.

Martin Fowler, "Dark Launching (bliki)", https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/DarkLaunching.html (2017) — Dark launch technique: validates new code under real production load with zero user exposure before progressive rollout.

ThoughtWorks, "Enabling Trunk Based Development with Deployment Pipelines", https://www.thoughtworks.com/insights/blog/enabling-trunk-based-development-deployment-pipelines (2015) — How feature toggles enable trunk-based development for teams practicing continuous delivery; hides unfinished features so incomplete code can be checked into main without exposing it to users.

Siddharth K. et al., "Piranha: Reducing Feature Flag Debt", https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3375716.3375764 (2020) — Automated AST-based refactoring tool that generated cleanup diffs for 1,381 stale flags at Uber; covers why stale flags accumulate, the cleanup workflow, and integration into developer pipelines.

Unleash, "11 Best Practices for Building and Scaling Feature Flag Systems", https://docs.getunleash.io/guides/feature-flag-best-practices (2024) — Open-source perspective on flag lifecycle: unique naming, short-lived defaults, availability over consistency, centralized evaluation logic, and systematic archiving.

GrowthBook, "The Engineer's Guide to Feature Flag Technical Debt", https://www.growthbook.io/resources/feature-flag-technical-debt (2026) — 2026 guide covering detection of stale flags, prevention strategies, automated cleanup workflows, and organizational practices for managing flag sprawl at scale.

Split.io, "Rollout Strategies for Faster Delivery With Feature Flags", https://medium.com/@SplitSoftware/rollout-strategies-for-faster-delivery-with-feature-flags-8f42b3260253 (2024) — Detailed rollout strategies including percentage rollouts, canary releases, and A/B testing with consistent bucketing; covers experiment invalidation and statistical validity.

LaunchDarkly, "Percentage rollouts", https://docs.launchdarkly.com/home/releases/percentage-rollouts/ — Official vendor documentation of deterministic percentage rollouts: hash partitions of 1-100,000 derived from context key, flag key and salt keep a context in the same bucket as the rollout percentage increases.

CNCF, "OpenFeature becomes a CNCF incubating project", https://www.cncf.io/blog/2023-12-19/openfeature-becomes-a-cncf-incubating-project/ (2023) — Vendor-neutral, open API for feature flagging standardised under the CNCF; one SDK interface in front of commercial, open-source or in-house flag backends removes vendor lock-in at the toggle point.

InfoQ, "When Feature Flags Go Wrong", https://www.infoq.com/articles/feature-flags-gone-wrong/ — Case-study critique of flag misuse: Knight Capital's $460M loss traced to a reused flag whose obsolete code path was still live, and LinkedIn's "flags all on" incident; argues for flag taxonomy, retirement and audit.

Anton Zaides, "Feature flags are ruining your codebase", https://zaidesanton.substack.com/p/feature-flags-are-ruining-your-codebase — Practitioner critique: flags multiply complexity, double the testing burden and hide bugs; reminders to remove flags rarely work, so expiry dates, active-flag caps and centralised ownership are required.
